events.title: Monteverdi's Orfeo Premieres
events.blurb: A 39-year-old Italian composer staged a setting of the Orpheus myth at a ducal palace in a northern Italian city, combining recitative, arias, choruses, and instrumental ritornellos in a way earlier experimental works had only gestured at. The resulting five-act piece is considered the first opera that remains in the regular performance repertoire. Only two printed scores of the work survive.
events.revealBlurb: February 24, 1607 — Claudio Monteverdi at the court of the Gonzagas in Mantua. The orchestra called for some 40 instruments. The character of Orpheus was sung by tenor Francesco Rasi; the audience was tiny — members of the Accademia degli Invaghiti.

events.title: Beethoven's Ninth Premieres
events.blurb: A nearly deaf 53-year-old composer, standing on the podium while a co-conductor did the actual directing, premiered a vast hour-long symphony that broke with convention by adding four vocal soloists and a chorus to the orchestra in its final movement. The text was a Schiller poem celebrating universal brotherhood. At the end the composer had to be turned around by one of the singers to see the audience — which he otherwise could not hear — thundering applause.
events.revealBlurb: May 7, 1824 — Ludwig van Beethoven at the Theater am Kärntnertor, Vienna. He had been profoundly deaf for over a decade. The "Ode to Joy" theme is now, somewhat jarringly given the text, the official anthem of the European Union.

events.title: Tchaikovsky's 1812 Overture Premieres
events.blurb: A Russian composer's commissioned patriotic overture commemorating the defeat of a Napoleonic invasion premiered at the consecration of a vast new Moscow cathedral. The score called for sixteen cannons fired in rhythm, a brass band to play "God Save the Tsar," and the bells of every church in the city ringing at the finale. The composer considered the whole thing hack-work and was embarrassed by its popularity.
events.revealBlurb: August 20, 1882 — Pyotr Tchaikovsky at the Cathedral of Christ the Saviour, Moscow. The cathedral was blown up by Stalin in 1931 and rebuilt in the 1990s. American Independence Day concerts have used the cannons since a 1974 Boston Pops performance under Arthur Fiedler.

events.title: The Rite of Spring Riot
events.blurb: A 30-year-old Russian composer's ballet score, depicting a pagan spring ritual with jagged rhythms, dissonant chord stacks, and primitivist choreography, premiered at a new Paris theatre and nearly caused a full-scale audience riot. Shouts, whistles, and fistfights broke out within minutes; the choreographer had to shout counts to dancers from the wings because they couldn't hear the orchestra. The piece is now considered one of the pivotal works of 20th-century music.
events.revealBlurb: May 29, 1913 — Igor Stravinsky and Ballets Russes at Théâtre des Champs-Élysées, Paris. Choreography by Vaslav Nijinsky. The Parisian critic Carl Van Vechten reported his seat-neighbour beating rhythmically on his head with his fists in distress.

events.title: Dark Side of the Moon Released
events.blurb: An English progressive rock band released a conceptual album about madness, mortality, capitalism, and the passage of time, tracks flowing into each other via tape loops of spoken voices, heartbeats, and cash registers. The cover was a simple black triangular prism refracting white light into a rainbow. The album would stay on the Billboard 200 for 741 consecutive weeks — more than 14 years — a record that has never been approached.
events.revealBlurb: March 1, 1973 — Pink Floyd. Recorded at Abbey Road using then-new 16-track technology and Roger Waters' theatrical sensibility. The album has sold over 45 million copies. The "we don't need no education" band followed eight years later with another cultural juggernaut, The Wall.

events.title: Space Invaders Hits Japanese Arcades
events.blurb: An alien formation that descended one row lower every time a column was destroyed — a quirk of the hardware clock — accidentally created the defining tension mechanic of arcade games. The game was so popular in Japan that bars converted into dedicated parlours.
events.revealBlurb: July 1978 — Taito released Space Invaders in Japan. The Atari 2600 home port in 1980 quadrupled console sales that year. The "yen coin shortage" is an urban legend — numismatists have found no evidence in mint records.

events.title: Asteroids Released by Atari
events.blurb: Drawing lines on a vector monitor to simulate drifting through space debris sounds modest. The game that resulted became Atari's best-selling arcade cabinet of all time, pulling in an estimated 10 million quarters per day at its peak. Demand was so extreme that Atari temporarily halted production of other games and shipped Asteroids units inside Lunar Lander cabinets just to get them out the door faster.
events.revealBlurb: November 1979 — Atari released Asteroids in North American arcades. It sold over 70,000 cabinets. The game's high score table was the first widely adopted public performance metric in gaming — and the first subject of documented high-score fraud.

events.title: Street Fighter II Released in Arcades
events.blurb: Eight distinct fighters, each with their own special moves activated by precise joystick motions, turned a local arcade into a public arena. Players lined their quarters on the cabinet bezel to declare "next game." The fighting game genre was born, arcade revenues spiked, and a competitive meta-game of frame-perfect inputs arose organically.
events.revealBlurb: February–March 1991 — Street Fighter II: The World Warrior released in North American arcades February 6 and in Japan March 7. The SNES port sold 6.3 million copies. The game is credited with single-handedly reviving the arcade industry.

events.title: Pokémon Red and Green Released in Japan
events.blurb: A game about capturing and training pocket monsters on a handheld with a dying link cable had been in development for six years and nearly bankrupted its studio twice. It released quietly on a console most retailers considered obsolete. Within months it had detonated into the fastest-growing entertainment franchise in Japanese history.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1996 — Pokémon Red and Green launched for Game Boy in Japan. By the end of 1996 they had sold 3.6 million copies in Japan alone; the franchise has since generated over $150 billion, making it the highest-grossing media franchise in history.

events.title: Oculus Rift Kickstarter Campaign Launches
events.blurb: A 19-year-old in his parents' garage had spent years building virtual reality headsets from scavenged parts. His Kickstarter campaign asked for $250,000 to build a developer kit. It raised $2.4 million from nearly 10,000 backers. Two years later, Facebook acquired his company for $2 billion.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 2012 — Palmer Luckey launched the Oculus Rift Kickstarter, raising 974% of its $250,000 goal. Facebook (now Meta) acquired Oculus VR in March 2014 for approximately $2 billion.

events.title: Hammurabi Stele Carved
events.blurb: A Babylonian king had 282 laws carved onto a 2.25-metre-tall pillar of black basalt, topped with a relief showing him receiving his authority from the seated sun god Shamash. The laws range from compensation for surgical malpractice to rules on bride prices, with the refrain "if… then" throughout. The stele was carried off as war booty to Susa 600 years later and discovered there in 1901.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1754 BCE — Hammurabi, 6th king of the First Babylonian Dynasty. "An eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth" comes from here — law 196. Now in the Louvre. A second copy with slight variations was later found and is in Istanbul.

events.title: Sistine Chapel Ceiling Unveiled
events.blurb: A 37-year-old Florentine sculptor, who had accepted a papal commission reluctantly after four years insisting he was not a painter, unveiled 500 square metres of freshly painted fresco covering the ceiling of a Vatican chapel. The work, which had taken four years, depicted nine scenes from Genesis surrounded by 300 figures. The artist had painted it while standing, not lying down as myth claims, his neck bent back for hours daily.
events.revealBlurb: October 31, 1512 — Michelangelo Buonarroti. He wrote a sonnet complaining of his neck: "I've grown a goiter by dwelling in this den… my beard turns up to heaven." Restoration between 1980 and 1994 revealed vivid colours under 400 years of candle smoke.

events.title: Vermeer's Girl with a Pearl Earring
events.blurb: A Dutch painter in his early thirties completed an intimate oil study on canvas of a young woman turning toward the viewer, her head covered in a blue and yellow turban, a single teardrop-shaped pearl catching the light at her ear. It was not a commissioned portrait but a "tronie" — a character study. The artist made only about 35 paintings in his career; this one was rediscovered in 1881 at auction for two guilders.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1665 — Johannes Vermeer. Now in the Mauritshuis in The Hague. The "pearl" may actually be tin or glass — no pearl of that size is plausible. Tracy Chevalier's 1999 novel and the 2003 film made it a pop-culture icon.

events.title: Mona Lisa Stolen
events.blurb: An Italian handyman who had worked at a Paris museum hid overnight in a storage closet, walked out the next morning in his worker's smock carrying a 77 by 53 cm wooden panel under his arm, and disappeared for two years and four months. The panel was a portrait by Leonardo da Vinci of a Florentine merchant's wife. The theft made worldwide news; Picasso and the poet Apollinaire were briefly questioned as suspects. The picture had been little known until this moment.
events.revealBlurb: August 21, 1911 — Vincenzo Peruggia. He was caught in Florence 28 months later trying to sell it to the Uffizi. He served seven months in Italian prison and was celebrated as a patriot by many Italians. The theft made the Mona Lisa internationally famous.

events.title: Pollock's Drip Paintings
events.blurb: A 35-year-old American painter, working in a converted barn studio on Long Island, laid large unstretched canvases on the floor and moved around their edges pouring and flinging paint from sticks and hardened brushes. The resulting "drip paintings" rejected representational composition entirely in favour of overall visual rhythm. A 1949 Life magazine spread asked: "Jackson Pollock: Is he the greatest living painter in the United States?" and made him instantly famous and nearly famously alcoholic.
events.revealBlurb: 1947 — Jackson Pollock began the drip technique in Springs, NY. He died in a car crash driving drunk on August 11, 1956, aged 44. His "No. 5, 1948" sold privately in 2006 for $140 million, briefly the highest price ever paid for a painting.

events.title: Kepler's Laws of Planetary Motion Published
events.blurb: A German mathematician published two laws describing how planets orbit the Sun: first, that orbits are ellipses with the Sun at one focus; second, that a line from the planet to the Sun sweeps equal areas in equal times — meaning planets move faster when close to the Sun. A third law, relating orbital period to distance, followed ten years later, providing the first precise mathematical description of the solar system.
events.revealBlurb: 1609 (laws 1&2) and 1619 (law 3) — Johannes Kepler derived the laws from the most precise observational data in the world, collected by Tycho Brahe. Brahe had guarded the data obsessively and refused to share it; Kepler obtained it only after Brahe's sudden death. He later calculated that Brahe may have died from a burst bladder after refusing to leave a banquet to use the lavatory.

events.title: Periodic Table of Elements Published
events.blurb: A Russian chemist arranged the sixty-three known elements into a table ordered by atomic weight, discovering that chemical properties recurred in a regular pattern. He boldly left gaps for elements he predicted did not yet exist, specifying their likely weights and properties in advance — predictions that proved startlingly accurate when the missing elements were found over the following two decades.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1869 — Dmitri Mendeleev reportedly saw the complete arrangement in a dream and woke to write it down, though historians treat this story sceptically. He sent a one-page summary to chemists across Europe before the formal presentation. Germanium, gallium, and scandium were discovered later, matching his predictions closely.

events.title: Special Relativity Paper Published
events.blurb: A 30-page paper demolished the concept of absolute time, arguing that the speed of light is the same for all observers regardless of their motion, and that simultaneity, length, and mass all depend on relative velocity. The paper contained no citations, because its author — a patent clerk working in his spare time — had arrived at the theory by pure thought experiment.
events.revealBlurb: September 26, 1905 — one of four papers the same author submitted to Annalen der Physik that year, including one on Brownian motion and one that would later win the Nobel Prize for the photoelectric effect. The mass-energy equivalence paper (E=mc²) followed two months later.

events.title: Pluto Discovered
events.blurb: A young farm-hand-turned-astronomer at an Arizona observatory found a faint, slowly moving point of light by comparing photographic plates taken several days apart — a new body at the edge of the solar system. The discovery completed a decadelong search for a hypothetical ninth planet believed to be perturbing the orbits of the outermost known worlds.
events.revealBlurb: February 18, 1930 — Clyde Tombaugh was 24 and had never attended university. The name "Pluto" was suggested by Venetia Burney, an 11-year-old girl in Oxford, via her grandfather. In 2006, the International Astronomical Union reclassified Pluto as a "dwarf planet," prompting widespread public outrage and several state legislatures to pass resolutions disagreeing.

events.title: Neutron Discovered
events.blurb: A British physicist bombarded beryllium with alpha particles and detected a neutral radiation that could knock protons out of paraffin wax with remarkable force. Reasoning that gamma rays lacked the energy for such collisions, he concluded the radiation must consist of uncharged particles with roughly the mass of a proton — completing the basic structure of the atomic nucleus.
events.revealBlurb: February 27, 1932 — James Chadwick completed the decisive experiments in under two weeks. He mailed a letter to Nature titled "Possible Existence of a Neutron." Frédéric and Irène Joliot-Curie had the same data a month earlier but misidentified what they had found. Chadwick won the Nobel Prize in 1935.

events.title: Iron Curtain Speech
events.blurb: A former British prime minister, speaking at a small college in Missouri at the invitation of the sitting U.S. president, declared that an impenetrable barrier had descended across the European continent from the Baltic to the Adriatic. The phrase he coined to describe it entered geopolitical vocabulary within hours.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1946 — Winston Churchill at Westminster College in Fulton, Missouri. Truman sat on stage behind him. The 5,000-word speech was titled "The Sinews of Peace," but nobody remembers that part.

events.title: Stalin Dies
events.blurb: Found unconscious on the floor of his dacha outside Moscow after a late-night dinner with colleagues, a dictator who had ruled for nearly three decades lingered for four days before dying of a brain hemorrhage. His inner circle, terrified of waking him, had delayed calling doctors for many hours. His state funeral drew crowds so large that dozens were trampled.
events.revealBlurb: March 5, 1953 — Joseph Stalin, 74, at his Kuntsevo dacha. He'd spent the previous evening screening American westerns. His death unleashed a succession struggle; Khrushchev prevailed and began the cautious thaw.

events.title: Berlin Wall Built
events.blurb: Overnight, East German soldiers and workers unrolled barbed wire along the jagged frontier between the two halves of a divided city, cutting off the escape route that some 3.5 million people had used to flee west over the previous twelve years. Within days the wire was replaced with concrete. Families woke to find themselves permanently separated from relatives one street away.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1961 — construction began at 2 AM on a Sunday. The wall eventually grew to 155 kilometres, with 302 watchtowers and a "death strip" of raked sand and trip-wires. At least 140 people died trying to cross it going west.

events.title: Prague Spring Invasion
events.blurb: Reform-minded leaders in a central European capital had spent eight months experimenting with "socialism with a human face" — easing censorship, rehabilitating purge victims, and tolerating debate. In the night, 250,000 Warsaw Pact soldiers and 2,000 tanks rolled across the borders. Unarmed civilians tried to argue with the invading soldiers; within days the reforms were reversed.
events.revealBlurb: August 20-21, 1968 — invasion of Czechoslovakia. Reformist leader Alexander Dubček was flown to Moscow and forced to sign a capitulation. A student named Jan Palach set himself on fire in Wenceslas Square five months later in protest.

events.title: Solidarity Founded
events.blurb: A strike at a shipyard in a Polish coastal city, led by an electrician who had been fired for union organizing, forced the communist government to sign an agreement permitting an independent, self-governing trade union — the first in the eastern bloc. Within a year ten million workers had joined. Martial law followed in December 1981, but the genie was out.
events.revealBlurb: August 31, 1980 — the Gdańsk Agreement. Electrician Lech Wałęsa would win the Nobel Peace Prize in 1983 and become Poland's first post-communist president in 1990. The movement's red logo, hand-painted in a shipyard, became an icon.

events.title: Jenner's First Vaccination
events.blurb: A 47-year-old English country doctor in Gloucestershire inoculated an 8-year-old boy with pus scraped from the hand of a milkmaid who had contracted cowpox, a mild disease related to smallpox but harmless in humans. Six weeks later he inoculated the boy with actual smallpox. The boy did not get sick. The doctor wrote up his results, which transformed public health across the world over the next two centuries.
events.revealBlurb: May 14, 1796 — Edward Jenner inoculated James Phipps. The word "vaccine" comes from vacca (Latin for cow). Jenner refused to patent the procedure despite the enormous potential fortune, insisting it was a gift to humanity. Smallpox was declared eradicated in 1980 — the only disease eliminated through vaccination.

events.title: Pasteur's Rabies Vaccine Used on a Human
events.blurb: A French chemist administered the first human dose of an experimental rabies treatment to a nine-year-old boy who had been severely bitten by a rabid dog two days earlier and faced certain death without intervention. The boy survived, and the successful case launched the practice of post-exposure vaccination for infectious disease.

events.title: Aspirin Marketed
events.blurb: A German pharmaceutical and dye company began commercial sales of acetylsalicylic acid tablets under a trade name they had registered, marketed initially as an analgesic and anti-inflammatory. The active compound had been synthesized decades earlier, but this company had developed a stable, pure form suitable for mass production. The drug became one of the best-selling over-the-counter medications in history; low-dose versions are now used preventively against cardiovascular disease.
events.revealBlurb: March 6, 1899 — Bayer AG. Chief chemist Felix Hoffmann is traditionally credited; some historians credit Arthur Eichengrün, a Jewish colleague whose role was erased under Nazi-era Bayer PR. The drug's trade name came from a combination of "acetyl" and Spiraea, a plant source of salicylic acid.

events.title: CRISPR-Cas9 Published
events.blurb: A team of molecular biologists led by a pair of American and French scientists published a paper in Science describing how a bacterial antiviral system — clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats and an enzyme — could be programmed in the laboratory to cut DNA at any desired sequence. The tool made gene editing orders of magnitude cheaper and faster than previous methods. A patent fight between two universities consumed much of the ensuing decade.
events.revealBlurb: June 28, 2012 — Jennifer Doudna (UC Berkeley), Emmanuelle Charpentier (Umeå). They shared the 2020 Nobel in Chemistry. Feng Zhang at the Broad Institute applied CRISPR to mammalian cells separately; the patent dispute over commercial rights has yet to be fully resolved.

events.title: First COVID-19 Vaccine Authorized
events.blurb: The US Food and Drug Administration issued an emergency use authorization for a novel mRNA-based vaccine against SARS-CoV-2, developed in less than a year from the publication of the virus's genetic sequence — a timescale previously thought impossible for a vaccine. The mRNA technology, which instructs the body's own cells to produce viral spike protein that the immune system then learns to recognize, had been in development for decades but had never been used in a licensed vaccine.
events.revealBlurb: December 11, 2020 — Pfizer-BioNTech vaccine. Moderna's similar mRNA vaccine followed December 18. Katalin Karikó and Drew Weissman, whose basic mRNA research had been neglected for years, won the 2023 Nobel Prize in Medicine. Over 13 billion COVID vaccine doses were administered globally in the first three years.

events.title: Jackie Robinson Breaks Color Barrier
events.blurb: A 28-year-old second baseman took the field at a Brooklyn ballpark and became the first African-American to play in modern Major League Baseball, breaking a 63-year color line enforced by gentlemen's agreement rather than written rule. He went hitless in his debut but reached base on an error and scored the winning run.
events.revealBlurb: April 15, 1947 — Ebbets Field, Brooklyn Dodgers. Team president Branch Rickey had signed him with the understanding he would absorb abuse without retaliation for two years. Robinson's number 42 was retired across every MLB team in 1997, the only such universal retirement in sports.

events.title: SNCC Founded
events.blurb: At a North Carolina conference convened by a veteran activist, 200 student sit-in leaders from across the South formed a new grassroots organization to coordinate direct-action campaigns independently of older civil rights groups. The students were younger, more confrontational, and willing to risk their lives; many became the foot soldiers of the Freedom Rides, Freedom Summer, and Selma.
events.revealBlurb: April 17, 1960 — Raleigh, NC. Student Nonviolent Coordinating Committee, commonly pronounced "snick." Organizer Ella Baker convinced the students to stay independent rather than fold into Martin Luther King's Southern Christian Leadership Conference. Stokely Carmichael led it during the "Black Power" turn in 1966.

events.title: Bloody Sunday in Selma
events.blurb: Six hundred civil-rights marchers, demanding federal protection for Black voting rights, set out from a small Alabama city to walk 87 kilometres to the state capital. On the Edmund Pettus Bridge at the edge of town, state troopers and a sheriff's posse on horseback charged them with clubs and tear gas. Televised images of a beaten John Lewis shocked the nation into action.
events.revealBlurb: March 7, 1965 — Selma, Alabama. Lewis's skull was fractured. Lyndon Johnson appeared before a joint session of Congress eight days later to introduce the Voting Rights Act, closing with the movement's own anthem: "We shall overcome."

events.title: Black Panther Party Founded
events.blurb: Two community-college students in a California Bay Area city drafted a ten-point program demanding full employment, decent housing, exemption from military service, and an end to police brutality for Black Americans. They organized armed neighborhood patrols to monitor police, opened free-breakfast programs for children, and ran medical clinics. The FBI declared them "the greatest threat to internal security" within four years.
events.revealBlurb: October 15, 1966 — Huey Newton and Bobby Seale in Oakland. J. Edgar Hoover's COINTELPRO infiltrated the party and fabricated rivalries between it and the US Organization; the free breakfasts, which he called "the greatest threat," fed 20,000 children a day at their peak.

events.title: Los Angeles Riots
events.blurb: Four police officers filmed beating a Black motorist named Rodney King for 81 seconds after a traffic chase were acquitted of assault by a jury with no Black members. Within hours, six days of rioting erupted across South Central Los Angeles. 63 people died, 2,383 were injured, and $1 billion in property damage was inflicted — making it the costliest civil disturbance in U.S. history.
events.revealBlurb: April 29 to May 4, 1992. King himself pleaded: "Can we all get along?" The officers were subsequently retried on federal civil rights charges; two were convicted. Korean-owned small businesses in "Koreatown" were disproportionately destroyed and inadequately protected.

events.title: First Networked Email
events.blurb: A computer engineer working for a Cambridge, Massachusetts research firm sent an electronic message between two computers sitting next to each other in his office, using a symbol from the typewriter keyboard he'd picked precisely because it was never used in names — the "at" sign — to separate the user name from the host machine name. He could not recall years later what the message had contained; probably "QWERTYUIOP" or similar.
events.revealBlurb: October 1971 — Ray Tomlinson at BBN Technologies. The @ symbol's adoption was arbitrary but lasting. Tomlinson's contribution is the reason your email address contains an @. He died in 2016.

events.title: Yahoo! Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford electrical engineering PhD students who had spent a year maintaining a website called "Jerry and David's guide to the World Wide Web" — a manually curated directory of interesting sites — incorporated their hobby as a business. They'd rename it with a word from Gulliver's Travels meaning an uncouth, rude person. For most of the decade, it was the default homepage of the internet.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 1995 — Jerry Yang and David Filo. The name is officially a backronym: "Yet Another Hierarchical Officious Oracle." They turned down a $44.6 billion acquisition offer from Microsoft in 2008; Verizon eventually bought the husk for $4.48 billion in 2017.

events.title: Google Incorporated
events.blurb: Two Stanford PhD students filed articles of incorporation for a search-engine company they had been developing in a dormitory and a rented garage in suburban California. Their algorithm, unlike those of competitors, ranked pages by how many other pages linked to them. They would never graduate. Their search index contained 60 million pages when they incorporated; it contains hundreds of billions today.
events.revealBlurb: September 4, 1998 — Larry Page and Sergey Brin. The name is a misspelling of "googol," the mathematical term for 10^100. Their initial financial backer, Sun Microsystems co-founder Andy Bechtolsheim, wrote a $100,000 check to "Google Inc." before the company formally existed.

events.title: Twitter's First Tweet
events.blurb: A 29-year-old podcasting-company engineer tested a prototype microblogging platform the team had built in two weeks as a side project, posting the five-word message "just setting up my twttr." Users were limited to 140 characters, the carrier limit for SMS text messages, since the service was originally designed to be usable by phone text. Within four years the service would be blamed — and credited — for upending journalism, politics, and activism.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 2006 — Jack Dorsey's first tweet. Co-founders included Biz Stone, Noah Glass, and Evan Williams. Elon Musk bought the company for $44 billion in 2022 and renamed it X the following year. Dorsey's original tweet was auctioned as an NFT for $2.9 million in 2021.

events.title: Ellen's Oscar Selfie
events.blurb: A television talk-show host hosting the annual U.S. film industry awards ceremony staged an elaborate star-packed selfie live on stage, tweeting it from her Samsung phone. The image was retweeted more than a million times within an hour, temporarily breaking the social network. The photo included thirteen people — three winners, seven nominees, two non-nominees, and the show's host. It held the record for most-retweeted photo for years.
events.revealBlurb: March 2, 2014 — Ellen DeGeneres at the 86th Academy Awards. The selfie was actually taken by Bradley Cooper. Samsung had paid $20 million for product placement on the telecast; arguably worth every dollar.

events.title: Battle of Tours
events.blurb: A Frankish mayor of the palace led an infantry army into a defensive wall of shields against a much larger Umayyad cavalry force that had been raiding deep into western Europe. The battle's outcome stopped the northward expansion of the Islamic caliphate into the Frankish heartland and established the Carolingian dynasty as the dominant power of the region.
events.revealBlurb: October 10, 732 — Charles Martel ("Charles the Hammer") in central France. His grandson Charlemagne would be crowned emperor 68 years later. Edward Gibbon later wrote that without the victory, "the interpretation of the Koran would now be taught in the schools of Oxford."

events.title: Charlemagne Crowned Emperor
events.blurb: A Frankish king, in a papal basilica in the old western imperial capital for Christmas Mass, rose from prayer to be unexpectedly crowned "Emperor of the Romans" by the pope. The coronation resurrected, at least in title, a western empire that had been extinct for 324 years, and established a relationship between popes and emperors that would shape European politics for eight centuries.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 800 — Charlemagne in Rome, crowned by Pope Leo III. Charlemagne later claimed he had been surprised — but the pope probably wouldn't have dared without his consent. The Holy Roman Empire survived in one form or another until 1806.

events.title: Genghis Khan Unites the Mongols
events.blurb: A 44-year-old tribal chieftain named Temüjin, having spent two decades defeating his rivals across the eastern steppe, was acclaimed "Universal Ruler" at an assembly of chieftains beside a sacred river. Within two decades his cavalry armies would sack Beijing, overrun Persia, and reach the Adriatic, creating the largest contiguous land empire in history.
events.revealBlurb: 1206 — at the Onon River. The title "Genghis Khan" is a western rendering; contemporary Mongol sources call him Činggis Qa'an. Genetic studies suggest roughly 16 million men alive today descend from his Y-chromosome line.

events.title: Avignon Papacy Begins
events.blurb: A French-born pope, under pressure from the French king and unable to safely reside in Rome because of factional warfare among Italian noble families, transferred the papal court across the Alps to a southern French town on the Rhône. For the next 68 years, seven successive popes — all French — would rule the Western church from there, deeply compromising papal prestige.
events.revealBlurb: 1309 — Pope Clement V. Critics called it the "Babylonian Captivity of the Church." The papacy returned to Rome in 1377, only to split almost immediately into rival popes in Rome and Avignon.

events.title: Siege of Orléans Lifted
events.blurb: A 17-year-old peasant girl from Lorraine, dressed in white armour and claiming visions from saints, led a French relief army into a besieged Loire Valley city. Over eight days of sorties, she personally led assaults on the English siege forts around the city, was shot through the shoulder with a crossbow bolt, returned to the fight, and broke the siege. The French war effort, exhausted for a generation, was transformed overnight.
events.revealBlurb: May 8, 1429 — Joan of Arc relieves Orléans. She had convinced a skeptical Dauphin to give her an army by passing a theological interrogation and, reportedly, a virginity test. She would see him crowned as Charles VII at Reims within ten weeks.

events.title: Bicycle Thieves Released
events.blurb: An Italian director released a quiet 89-minute film about an unemployed working-class man whose stolen bicycle means he cannot take a new job pasting posters on walls. The non-professional actors, documentary-style camera, and refusal of melodramatic conventions defined the Italian neorealist movement. The film spoke for a generation of post-war European audiences who had had enough of Hollywood glamour.
events.revealBlurb: November 24, 1948 — Vittorio De Sica. The father was played by a real factory worker; the son by a young boy De Sica spotted on the street. It won an honorary Academy Award before the foreign language category existed. Its influence on later directors — from Ken Loach to Satyajit Ray — is enormous.

events.title: Breathless Released
events.blurb: A 29-year-old French film critic turned director released a 90-minute crime film about a petty thief on the run in Paris with his American girlfriend, shot on handheld camera using natural light, jump cuts, and improvised dialogue. The film's insouciant rulebreaking embodied a new generation of European filmmaking, christened the "Nouvelle Vague" by a critic five years earlier. It made its star into the archetype of post-war cool.
events.revealBlurb: March 16, 1960 — Jean-Luc Godard, starring Jean-Paul Belmondo and Jean Seberg. The famously jarring jump-cuts emerged from an editing crisis: the film was too long and Godard simply removed shots rather than shorten scenes.

events.title: The Godfather Released
events.blurb: A 32-year-old American director of partial Italian descent, working on his third feature, released a 175-minute adaptation of a recent mass-market novel about an Italian-American crime family. His studio had imposed cast, budget, and length conditions throughout production; it had also tried to fire him multiple times. The film grossed more than any previous picture in history, won Best Picture, and launched decades of imitators that have never quite matched it.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1972 — Francis Ford Coppola. Marlon Brando's sagging jowls were created with dental plumpers; Al Pacino's casting was fought bitterly by Paramount executives who wanted Ryan O'Neal. The horse's head was real — acquired from a dog-food plant.

events.title: Apocalypse Now Released
events.blurb: An American director released a 153-minute film loosely adapting Joseph Conrad's "Heart of Darkness" to the context of the Vietnam War, shot over 238 days in the Philippines through a typhoon that destroyed much of the set, an on-set heart attack for his leading man, and a drug-fueled spiral for his support cast. He screened a rough cut at Cannes with the warning: "My film is not about Vietnam. My film is Vietnam."
events.revealBlurb: August 15, 1979 — Francis Ford Coppola, starring Martin Sheen and Marlon Brando. The documentary "Hearts of Darkness" chronicles the production's mayhem. Brando arrived on set overweight and unprepared; Coppola had to shoot him in shadow from the shoulders up.

events.title: Jurassic Park Released
events.blurb: A 46-year-old director released an adaptation of a recent Michael Crichton novel about genetically resurrected dinosaurs on a tropical-island theme park. The film's digital dinosaurs — only a few minutes of CGI, mixed with extensive full-size animatronic puppets — changed the calculus of what visual effects could do. Audiences gasped at a Tyrannosaurus rex roaring over a rain-soaked jeep; a decade of purely physical-effects films were obsolete.
events.revealBlurb: June 11, 1993 — Steven Spielberg. The T. rex breaking into the jeep was actually animatronic; it malfunctioned often in the Hawaii humidity. The film displaced E.T. as highest-grossing ever. Spielberg was editing "Schindler's List" at night during production.

events.title: Hindenburg Disaster
events.blurb: A German passenger airship, the largest aircraft ever flown, caught fire as it approached its mooring mast at a New Jersey naval air station, and was consumed in less than 40 seconds. 36 of the 97 people on board died, along with one ground crew member. A radio reporter's anguished live commentary — "Oh, the humanity!" — entered popular idiom.
events.revealBlurb: May 6, 1937 — Lakehurst, NJ. The reporter was Herbert Morrison; he was actually there to record for later broadcast and didn't expect to be on air. The disaster effectively killed the commercial airship industry overnight.

events.title: Mount St. Helens Eruption
events.blurb: A Pacific Northwest volcano that had been swelling a grotesque 150-metre bulge on its north flank for two months underwent a catastrophic lateral blast triggered by an earthquake. The collapse produced the largest landslide in recorded history, flattening 600 square kilometres of forest and killing 57 people, including a stubborn innkeeper who refused to evacuate.
events.revealBlurb: May 18, 1980 — Washington State, USA. The innkeeper was Harry R. Truman, 83, who kept pets and a collection of bourbon at his lodge and became a folk hero for his refusal to leave. His body was never found.

events.title: Bhopal Disaster
events.blurb: A cloud of methyl isocyanate gas leaked from a pesticide plant on the outskirts of a central Indian city shortly after midnight, drifting over densely populated slums whose inhabitants woke choking and blind. Between 8,000 and 16,000 people died in the immediate aftermath; 500,000 were injured. Groundwater at the site remains contaminated four decades on.
events.revealBlurb: December 2-3, 1984 — Bhopal, Madhya Pradesh. The plant was owned by Union Carbide; the American parent company settled for $470 million, a fraction of the actual cost. The CEO, Warren Anderson, was briefly arrested and then quietly released; India's extradition requests were ignored.

events.title: Tōhoku Earthquake & Fukushima
events.blurb: A magnitude 9.1 undersea earthquake off the Pacific coast of northern Japan triggered tsunami waves up to 40 metres high that killed some 19,700 people and swamped the seawalls of a coastal nuclear plant. Three reactor cores melted down in the following days, contaminating 337 square kilometres of surrounding countryside. 165,000 people were displaced; many never returned.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2011 — 2:46 PM local time. The quake was so powerful it shifted Earth's axis by about 17 centimetres and shortened the day by 1.8 microseconds. The plant's operator, TEPCO, had been warned about tsunami risk years earlier and ignored it.

events.title: COVID-19 Pandemic Declared
events.blurb: The World Health Organization, having watched a novel coronavirus spread from a single city to 114 countries in ten weeks, formally upgraded its assessment from epidemic to pandemic. Within days, much of the world entered some form of lockdown — schools shut, flights grounded, stock markets crashed. Before vaccines arrived a year later, it would kill millions.
events.revealBlurb: March 11, 2020 — WHO Director-General Tedros Adhanom Ghebreyesus. The first known case had been reported in Wuhan in early December 2019. Official global death toll exceeded 7 million; excess mortality studies suggest the real number is closer to 20 million.

events.title: Alam Ara Released — India's First Talkie
events.blurb: Police were deployed outside Majestic Cinema in Bombay that afternoon because the crowds gathering to hear a Hindi film speak for the first time overwhelmed the streets. The fantasy-romance had seven songs, making it arguably the first Bollywood musical; screenings sold out continuously for eight weeks, and the print of the film has since been completely lost.
events.revealBlurb: March 14, 1931 — directed by Ardeshir Irani. The film was shot in just 40 days. Every surviving account describes the audience's shock at hearing dialogue emerge from the screen, many reportedly weeping.

events.title: First Filmfare Awards Ceremony
events.blurb: A British-origin film magazine inaugurated India's first popular film awards at Bombay's Metro Theatre with only five categories, winners chosen through postal ballot by readers, and a chief guest who was the US Ambassador to India. The trophy — a black-painted female figure — later became among the most recognisable objects in the entire industry and came to be known, simply, as the Black Lady.
events.revealBlurb: March 21, 1954 — then called the "Clare Awards" after a recently deceased film critic. Best Film went to Bimal Roy's Do Bigha Zamin; Dilip Kumar won Best Actor for Daag. The ceremony's postal-ballot system meant the public, not critics, decided the winners — a populist structure the awards kept for decades.

events.title: Hum Aapke Hain Koun..! Released
events.blurb: A fourteen-song, over-three-hour family wedding drama that critics pre-screened and privately predicted was an unreleasable disaster became, on release, the first Hindi film to gross ₹1 billion — selling 74 million tickets domestically, the highest footfall for any Hindi film since the 1990s. The industry pivoted overnight toward family-oriented, non-violent spectacle.
events.revealBlurb: August 5, 1994 — director Sooraj Barjatya, a sequel of sorts to his earlier Maine Pyar Kiya. Salman Khan and Madhuri Dixit were cast against type as wholesome leads. The film ran in a Mumbai multiplex for over three years without leaving screens.

events.title: Taare Zameen Par Released
events.blurb: A film about an eight-year-old with undiagnosed dyslexia shipped off to boarding school for failing every subject — told largely from the child's hallucinatory perspective — earned ₹98 crore worldwide and prompted school boards across India to introduce dyslexia screening. Its child lead, discovered through an open casting call, had never acted before.
events.revealBlurb: December 21, 2007 — Aamir Khan's directorial debut, having taken over from Amole Gupte mid-production. Darsheel Safary, then 9, auditioned among 1,000 children. The film catalysed new Indian legislation on learning disability accommodation in schools. Khan dedicated the film to every child who had been misunderstood.

events.title: "Naatu Naatu" Wins Academy Award
events.blurb: A Telugu period action film about two real freedom fighters reimagined as friends on opposite sides of a colonial conflict produced a seven-minute dance sequence that, when performed live at the Dolby Theatre in Los Angeles, brought an Oscars audience to its feet. The song became the first from an Indian film to win the Academy Award for Best Original Song.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 2023 — the 95th Academy Awards. Composer M.M. Keeravani and lyricist Chandrabose won. Director S.S. Rajamouli's RRR had not been submitted as India's official Oscar entry — it qualified independently through its US distributor. Singers Rahul Sipligunj and Kaala Bhairava performed barefoot on the Oscars stage.

events.title: Monroe Doctrine Declared
events.blurb: An American president's annual address to Congress warned European powers against further colonization or political interference in the Western Hemisphere, a policy the United States could not yet militarily enforce but would cite for the next two centuries. The message was drafted largely by his Secretary of State, a future president himself.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1823 — James Monroe. The phrase "Monroe Doctrine" wasn't coined until 1850. Britain quietly backed the policy because it suited their own trade interests, and for decades the Royal Navy did most of the actual enforcing.

events.title: Iran Hostage Crisis Begins
events.blurb: Iranian students stormed the U.S. Embassy in Tehran and seized 52 American diplomats and staff as hostages, demanding that the United States extradite the deposed Shah — who was receiving cancer treatment in New York — and return his assets. The hostages were held for 444 days, paralyzing the Carter presidency and reshaping American politics for a generation.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 1979 — Tehran, Iran. The hostages were released on January 20, 1981 — literally within minutes of Ronald Reagan being inaugurated. Carter spent his last night as president awake, monitoring the negotiations.

events.title: U.S. Invades Iraq
events.blurb: A U.S.-led coalition launched air strikes and a ground invasion of Iraq in a "shock and awe" campaign code-named Operation Iraqi Freedom, premised on intelligence assessments — later found to be wrong — that Saddam Hussein possessed weapons of mass destruction. The initial combat phase lasted 41 days; the subsequent occupation and insurgency lasted until 2011 and killed more than 4,400 American service members.
events.revealBlurb: March 20, 2003 — Baghdad, Iraq. No weapons of mass destruction were found. Saddam Hussein was captured hiding in a hole near Tikrit in December 2003 and executed by hanging in December 2006. President Bush declared "Mission Accomplished" on May 1, 2003, from the deck of an aircraft carrier; the war continued for eight more years.

events.title: Barack Obama Elected President
events.blurb: A first-term U.S. senator, 47 years old and the son of a Kenyan father and Kansan mother, defeated his Republican opponent by a nine-million-vote margin to become the 44th President of the United States and the first Black person elected to the office. He carried states no Democrat had won in decades, including Indiana and North Carolina.
events.revealBlurb: November 4, 2008 — defeating John McCain. Obama gave his victory speech in Chicago's Grant Park before 200,000 people. Jesse Jackson, standing in the crowd, wept on camera. Michelle Obama became the first African-American First Lady.

events.title: COVID-19 National Emergency Declared
events.blurb: President Donald Trump declared a national emergency, unlocking $50 billion in federal disaster funds to respond to the coronavirus pandemic, which had by then spread to 49 states and killed dozens of Americans. The pandemic would ultimately claim over 1.1 million American lives — more than any war in the country's history — and shut down schools, businesses, and public life for over a year.
events.revealBlurb: March 13, 2020 — The White House. The first confirmed U.S. case had been detected just 53 days earlier. Within weeks, American unemployment reached 14.7% — the highest since the Great Depression — as roughly 22 million jobs vanished in two months.

events.title: Gallic Sack of Rome
events.blurb: Senone Gauls under their chieftain Brennus routed a Roman army at the Allia River, then entered a largely deserted Rome three days later and burned it for seven months. The sole holdout was the Capitoline Hill, where a sacred flock of geese allegedly woke the defenders when a Gallic night-assault crept up the cliffs.
events.revealBlurb: July 390 BCE, traditional (Polybius says 387). The ransom Brennus demanded in gold was agreed, but the Romans protested he was using rigged weights. Brennus reportedly threw his sword onto the scales and bellowed "Vae victis" — "Woe to the vanquished."

events.title: Assassination of Julius Caesar
events.blurb: A group of Roman senators led by Cassius and Brutus surrounded the dictator in the Theatre of Pompey and stabbed him twenty-three times. A later physician concluded only one wound was fatal; the man fell at the base of a statue of his former rival, Pompey himself.
events.revealBlurb: The Ides of March, 44 BCE. Caesar had been warned by a soothsayer to "beware the Ides of March" and laughed it off the same morning. His last words, "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare — ancient sources quote him saying "You too, child?" in Greek.

events.title: Death of Marcus Aurelius
events.blurb: The philosopher-emperor Marcus Aurelius died of illness at the Danubian frontier, most likely at Vindobona, at the age of 58 after nineteen years of near-constant warfare against Germanic tribes. He chose to pass the empire to his biological son Commodus rather than adopt a capable successor, ending the run of four successive emperors who had done exactly that.
events.revealBlurb: March 17, 180 CE. Marcus kept a private notebook of philosophical reflections — the Meditations — with no apparent intention of publication. One entry reads: "Loss is nothing else but change, and change is Nature's delight." He died of the same plague he had spent a decade governing around.

events.title: Julian the Apostate's Pagan Revival
events.blurb: Emperor Julian — Constantine's nephew, raised as a Christian — publicly renounced Christianity upon taking power, reopened pagan temples that had been confiscated or closed, restored their revenues, and barred Christians from teaching classical literature in schools. He lasted only eighteen months before dying from a spear wound during a Persian campaign.
events.revealBlurb: November 361 CE. Julian wrote philosophical treatises, got up before dawn to perform sacrifices, and reportedly sacrificed so many oxen that soldiers nicknamed him "the Slaughterhouse." His pagan restoration died with him; every successor returned to Christianity.

events.title: Vandal Sack of Rome
events.blurb: King Gaiseric sailed from Carthage, landed at Ostia at the mouth of the Tiber, and marched his Vandal army into Rome unopposed. Pope Leo I negotiated terms again — no killing, no burning — but the Vandals then spent two full weeks systematically stripping the city of everything portable: gilded bronze roof tiles from the Temple of Jupiter, treasures from the imperial palace, and thousands of enslaved captives.
events.revealBlurb: June 455 CE. The Vandals' two-week methodical looting is considered more destructive than Alaric's three-day sack of 410. The stripping of the Temple of Jupiter's gilded roof tiles — a deliberate act of de-monumentalisation — gave Western languages the word "vandalism."

events.title: Intel 4004 Microprocessor Released
events.blurb: Intel released a 4-bit central processing unit containing 2,300 transistors on a silicon chip the size of a fingernail, capable of 60,000 operations per second. Originally designed for a Japanese calculator company, it became the world's first commercially available microprocessor — the prototype for every CPU that followed.

events.title: Macintosh Launched
events.blurb: A California computer company launched a new desktop computer during a Super Bowl advertising spot, and formally introduced it at a shareholders meeting two days later. The machine had a 9-inch black-and-white screen, a mouse, a graphical user interface with icons and windows, and pull-down menus — none of which had previously shipped on a mass-market computer. It cost $2,495 and would struggle commercially against the cheaper IBM PC for years.
events.revealBlurb: January 24, 1984 — Apple Macintosh. Ridley Scott's "1984" Super Bowl ad ran on January 22. The original Mac shipped with 128KB of memory; Bill Gates had quietly promised Steve Jobs a version of MS Word for it.

events.title: Intel Pentium Released
events.blurb: A Silicon Valley chipmaker released the fifth generation of its mass-market microprocessor under the brand name "Pentium" — a word coined to be trademarkable, since numerical names like "586" were not. The chip included 3.1 million transistors and outperformed its 486 predecessor by a factor of two. A subtle floating-point division bug discovered by a math professor the following year forced a $475 million recall.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1993 — Intel Pentium (P5). The floating-point bug (the FDIV bug) was discovered by Thomas Nicely of Lynchburg College. Initially Intel offered replacements only to customers who could prove they used the chip for heavy math. Bad PR forced full replacement.

events.title: Google Founded
events.blurb: Two Stanford doctoral students incorporated a search engine company whose name derived from the mathematical term for 10 to the power of 100. Their PageRank algorithm ranked results by treating hyperlinks as votes, producing more relevant results than the keyword-frequency systems that dominated at the time.

events.title: AlphaGo Beats Lee Sedol
events.blurb: A London-based artificial intelligence laboratory's go-playing program, trained on millions of human games and then on games it had played against itself, defeated the reigning world champion of the ancient Asian board game 4–1 in a five-game match in Seoul. The match was broadcast live to 280 million people. Experts had predicted a champion-beating go program was a decade away; the algorithmic gap between games like chess and go had seemed insurmountable.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 2016 — DeepMind's AlphaGo vs. Lee Sedol. Lee's single winning game, move 78 — the "divine move" — exploited a subtle blind spot in the AI. DeepMind was acquired by Google in 2014 for around $500 million. Lee retired from professional go three years later, partly because AI had changed the game.

events.title: First Spacewalk
events.blurb: Soviet cosmonaut Alexei Leonov floated outside Voskhod 2 through an inflatable airlock and spent 12 minutes and 9 seconds in open space — the first human extravehicular activity. His spacesuit then ballooned in the vacuum to the point where he could no longer fit back through the hatch, forcing him to bleed pressure from a valve before squeezing inside headfirst.
events.revealBlurb: March 18, 1965 — Voskhod 2. The suit's engineers had fitted it with a built-in suicide pill. Leonov later said sweat filled his boots to the knee from the exertion of forcing himself back in. The spacecraft also drifted into an unplanned orbit and landed 386 km off target in the Ural mountains, where the crew spent a night in wolf country.

events.title: First Soft Moon Landing
events.blurb: The Soviet Luna 9 spacecraft landed intact on the Ocean of Storms, becoming the first vehicle to achieve a controlled soft landing on another world and transmit photographs from the surface. Its four petal-shaped panels opened to right the lander and deploy an antenna, then it sent back a panoramic image sequence over three sessions totaling nine images.
events.revealBlurb: February 3, 1966 — Luna 9. British radio astronomers at Jodrell Bank intercepted the transmission and noticed it used the same format as a standard wire-photo machine. They borrowed a Müller facsimile unit from a news agency and published the images before the Soviets released them officially — to Moscow's considerable irritation.

events.title: Challenger Disintegration
events.blurb: Space Shuttle Challenger broke apart 73 seconds after launch when a rubber O-ring seal on the right solid rocket booster failed in overnight temperatures that had dropped to -8 °C, allowing combustion gases to breach the joint and sever the external tank. All seven crew members were killed, including Christa McAuliffe, who had been selected from more than 11,000 applicants for NASA's Teacher in Space program.
events.revealBlurb: January 28, 1986 — STS-51-L. Engineers at Morton Thiokol had urged a launch delay the night before, citing O-ring behavior in cold temperatures; NASA managers overruled them. The crew cabin survived the initial breakup intact and fell for nearly three minutes before striking the Atlantic at roughly 320 km/h.

events.title: Mir Space Station Deorbit
events.blurb: Russia deliberately deorbited the Mir space station after 15 years of continuous operation, using three burns from a docked Progress cargo spacecraft to lower its orbit until it reentered the atmosphere over the South Pacific. Most of the station burned up during reentry, but approximately 1,500 kg of debris survived and splashed into the ocean between Australia and Chile.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 2001 — Mir deorbit. Mir had been in orbit so long that cosmonauts reported the walls were alive with mold. A Russian company sold pay-per-view rights to watch the reentry from a chartered aircraft. Japan offered to purchase and keep the station operational; the deal fell through over cost. It had been visited by 104 cosmonauts and astronauts from 12 nations.

events.title: Chang'e 4 Far Side Moon Landing
events.blurb: China's Chang'e 4 lander and Yutu-2 rover touched down in the Von Kármán Crater within the South Pole–Aitken Basin, the oldest and largest impact crater in the solar system, becoming the first spacecraft ever to land on the lunar far side. Because the far side never faces Earth, the mission required a dedicated relay satellite positioned at the Moon–Earth L2 point to maintain communications.
events.revealBlurb: January 3, 2019 — Chang'e 4. The far side of the Moon faces away from Earth permanently due to tidal locking — no human-made object had ever touched it before. The Yutu-2 rover discovered an unusually viscous material in a small crater that scientists believe may be impact-melted basalt glass. It remains operational, the longest-running lunar rover in history.

events.title: Salt March Begins
events.blurb: A 60-year-old lawyer in a homespun loincloth set out from his ashram with 78 followers to walk 390 kilometres to the coast, intending to violate a colonial monopoly by picking up a pinch of seawater-evaporated salt. The 24-day trek grew into a procession of thousands; the defiance of the salt law spread across the country within weeks. 60,000 Indians, including the leader himself, were jailed within three months.
events.revealBlurb: March 12, 1930 — Gandhi begins the Dandi March from Sabarmati Ashram. Newspapers across the world carried photographs of him scooping up salt on the beach on April 6. Winston Churchill, watching from Westminster, privately described the prospect of "seditious middle-temple lawyer" meeting the viceroy as nauseating.

events.title: Bhagat Singh Executed
events.blurb: Three young revolutionaries were hanged an hour earlier than scheduled at a jail in a Punjabi city, after a three-year trial for killing a British police officer they had mistaken for the superintendent they had meant to assassinate. The youngest of them was 23. Crowds had gathered outside the prison expecting the normal morning execution time; by the time they arrived, the bodies had already been smuggled out and cremated by the riverside.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1931 — Bhagat Singh, Rajguru, and Sukhdev at Lahore Central Jail. Their martyrdom made them arguably the most venerated revolutionaries of the independence movement, an icon Gandhi's non-violent path never quite matched among the young.

events.title: Indian Independence & Partition
events.blurb: At the stroke of midnight, two new independent dominions came into existence on the subcontinent — one majority-Hindu, one majority-Muslim — as the British flag was lowered on the largest and oldest of Britain's imperial possessions. The division of provinces along religious lines displaced between 10 and 20 million people, and perhaps a million died in the communal violence that followed.
events.revealBlurb: August 14-15, 1947 — Pakistan on the 14th, India on the 15th. The boundary lines had been drawn by a London barrister, Cyril Radcliffe, who had never visited the subcontinent and had 36 days to complete the task. Nehru's "Tryst with Destiny" speech was delivered at midnight from the Constituent Assembly.

events.title: Indo-Pakistani War of 1965
events.blurb: Infiltrators crossed the ceasefire line into a disputed northern territory to incite a rebellion that failed to materialize. India retaliated by invading across the international border toward a major Pakistani city. Seventeen days of conventional ground and air combat across the Punjab plains ended in stalemate, with each side convinced it had won. 3,000 Indian and 3,800 Pakistani soldiers died.
events.revealBlurb: August-September 1965 — ended by the Tashkent Declaration in January. The Battle of Asal Uttar saw one of the largest tank battles since WWII. Neither side's territorial changes amounted to much, and what they gained was returned at Tashkent.

events.title: Pokhran-II Nuclear Tests
events.blurb: India conducted five underground nuclear explosions over two days in the same Rajasthani desert test range it had used 24 years earlier, including a claimed thermonuclear device. The tests, carried out in conditions of extraordinary operational security that surprised American intelligence satellites, declared the country a full nuclear-weapon state. Pakistan tested its own devices 17 days later.
events.revealBlurb: May 11 and 13, 1998 — code-named Operation Shakti. Prime Minister Atal Bihari Vajpayee had been in office three months. Sanctions were imposed; they were lifted within two years as the United States reassessed its South Asia policy.

events.title: Great Wall of China Begun
events.blurb: The first emperor of a unified Chinese state, having conquered the six rival warring kingdoms, ordered existing regional defensive walls in the north linked into a continuous frontier fortification against nomadic incursions. A conscripted army of 300,000 labourers worked for years; many died on the project and were, according to tradition, buried in its foundations. The Ming-dynasty wall, which is what most modern visitors see, was rebuilt over a millennium later.
events.revealBlurb: c. 220 BCE — Qin Shi Huang. The visible stone-and-brick wall is largely Ming-dynasty (1368-1644), built with much better materials. The Qin wall was mostly earthen and only fragments survive. Total length, across all versions, has been measured at 21,196 km.

events.title: Hagia Sophia Consecrated
events.blurb: A vast domed cathedral, built in a Bosphorus imperial capital in just five years by 10,000 labourers, was consecrated with a grand procession. Its 31-metre-diameter dome seemed to float on light — a feat of engineering that would not be surpassed in Europe for nearly a thousand years. The emperor who commissioned it allegedly exclaimed: "Solomon, I have surpassed thee!"
events.revealBlurb: December 27, 537 — Constantinople (now Istanbul), under Justinian I. Architects were Anthemius of Tralles and Isidore of Miletus, both mathematicians. Converted to a mosque in 1453, a museum in 1934, and a mosque again in 2020.

events.title: Angkor Wat Completed
events.blurb: A Khmer king completed a vast temple complex in his capital, originally dedicated to the Hindu god Vishnu and later converted to Buddhist use. Covering over 160 hectares, surrounded by a moat, topped with a central tower 65 metres high, and decorated with 1.6 kilometres of bas-relief carvings illustrating Hindu epics, it was the largest religious monument in the world. After the Khmer capital shifted in the 15th century, the jungle gradually overgrew the complex, which was rediscovered by European travellers in the 19th century.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1150 — King Suryavarman II, in the capital of the Khmer Empire (modern Cambodia). It appears on the Cambodian flag — the only national flag featuring a building. French explorer Henri Mouhot's 1861 account brought it to Western attention, though it had never actually been "lost."

events.title: US Capitol Cornerstone Laid
events.blurb: The president of the newly independent United States — wearing a Masonic apron — laid the cornerstone of a new federal capitol building on a wooded hill above the banks of the Potomac River. The building was meant to house the U.S. Congress. The winning design, by a Scottish-trained amateur architect, was a neoclassical rotunda crowned with a low dome; later architects would replace the dome with a much taller cast-iron one during the Civil War.
events.revealBlurb: September 18, 1793 — George Washington at Jenkins Hill (now Capitol Hill), Washington, D.C. Designer: William Thornton. The current wedding-cake dome was built 1855-1866 by Thomas U. Walter and crowned with the Statue of Freedom during the Civil War. Slave labour built much of the original building.

events.title: Sagrada Família Begun
events.blurb: Construction began on a Catholic basilica in the Catalan capital, funded by donations alone — a condition that would stretch the project across a century and a half. The original architect was replaced after one year by a 31-year-old ferociously religious designer who would pour the rest of his life into the project, combining Gothic and Art Nouveau influences into a style of his own. He would die 43 years later, hit by a tram on the street outside; only a fraction of the church was finished. Construction continues today.
events.revealBlurb: March 19, 1882 — original architect Francisco de Paula del Villar; succeeded 1883 by Antoni Gaudí. Gaudí devoted the last 15 years of his life exclusively to the project. He was hit by a tram on June 7, 1926; his grave is in the crypt. Completion is projected for 2026 — a century after his death.

events.title: Gutenberg Bible Completed
events.blurb: A German goldsmith completed printing a 1,286-page Latin Bible using a press with movable metal type, producing an estimated 180 copies at a rate no scribe could approach. Each sheet required individually set letter blocks cast in an alloy of lead, tin, and antimony — making it the first book in Europe produced by mechanical movable type.

events.title: Columbus Reaches the Americas
events.blurb: A Genoese navigator captaining three small Spanish ships, after 33 days of open-Atlantic sailing from the Canary Islands with an increasingly mutinous crew, sighted land just after 2 AM — a low-lying island he promptly named after a Christian saviour. He was convinced, and would die still convinced, that he had reached the outer islands of Asia. The four voyages he made over the next twelve years reshaped two continents.
events.revealBlurb: October 12, 1492 — Christopher Columbus made landfall on Guanahani in the Bahamas. The lookout who first sighted land, Rodrigo de Triana, did not receive the promised reward — Columbus claimed he had seen a light the previous evening. The contact collapsed Indigenous populations via epidemic disease within decades.

events.title: Fall of Tenochtitlán
events.blurb: After a three-month siege — during which Spanish-allied Indigenous forces demolished the city district by district, channeled the causeways, and introduced a devastating smallpox epidemic — the last Aztec emperor surrendered in a canoe on the lake as his capital burned. The Spaniards, led by Cortés, renamed the ruins and built a viceregal capital on them. The Aztec empire ceased to exist; the Spanish conquest of the Americas was underway.
events.revealBlurb: August 13, 1521 — Cuauhtémoc surrendered to Cortés. The city's population had dropped from perhaps 200,000 to under 50,000 through disease, siege starvation, and fighting. The Spanish built Mexico City on the drained lakebed — which continues to sink today at 50 cm per year.

events.title: Copernicus's De Revolutionibus
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Polish mathematician and canon of a cathedral in Warmia died on the same day he was reportedly handed a freshly printed copy of the book he had been writing, revising, and withholding from publication for three decades. The book, On the Revolutions of the Heavenly Spheres, argued that the earth was a planet orbiting the sun, and that the apparent daily motion of the heavens was actually the earth's own rotation. It was placed on the Papal Index 73 years later.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1543 — Nicolaus Copernicus died. The book's printer, Andreas Osiander, had added an anonymous preface describing its heliocentrism as a mere mathematical convenience; Copernicus probably never saw that preface. Galileo, who openly defended heliocentrism, was tried for heresy in 1633.

events.title: Dutch East India Company Founded
events.blurb: The Dutch government chartered a joint-stock corporation with a 21-year monopoly on Asian trade, the authority to wage war, build forts, coin money, and conclude treaties in the name of the States General. It was the world's first publicly traded multinational corporation. Within decades it dominated the Asian spice trade, conquered chunks of Southeast Asia, and declared its own wars. At its height its market capitalization exceeded that of the combined top ten companies of today.
events.revealBlurb: March 20, 1602 — Verenigde Oostindische Compagnie (VOC). It employed over 70,000 people at its peak. Its share price rose 1,200 percent in the 1600s and collapsed in 1799 when the company was bankrupted by corruption, wars, and changing trade patterns.

events.title: British Parliament Passes the Stamp Act
events.blurb: Parliament enacted a sweeping tax requiring colonists to purchase revenue stamps for newspapers, legal documents, almanacs, and even playing cards — the first direct tax Britain had ever levied on its American colonies. Outcry was immediate and visceral: colonial assemblies passed resolutions of protest, merchants organized boycotts, and a new network of radicals calling themselves the Sons of Liberty took to the streets.
events.revealBlurb: March 22, 1765 — London. The tax was repealed the following year under merchant pressure, but Parliament simultaneously passed the Declaratory Act asserting its absolute right to tax the colonies "in all cases whatsoever." The colonists celebrated the repeal and mostly ignored the Declaratory Act — for about a decade.

events.title: Cherokee Removal Begins: Trail of Tears
events.blurb: The U.S. Army began forcibly rounding up approximately 15,000 Cherokee from their ancestral lands in Georgia, Tennessee, and North Carolina, interning them in stockades before marching them over 1,000 miles to Indian Territory in present-day Oklahoma. Estimates of deaths on the journey range from 4,000 to 6,000 — roughly one quarter of the entire Cherokee nation — from disease, exposure, and starvation.
events.revealBlurb: May 1838 — Georgia. The Cherokee had adopted a written constitution, built schools, published a newspaper, and won a Supreme Court ruling (Worcester v. Georgia) confirming their sovereignty. President Andrew Jackson simply ignored the Court. Chief Justice Marshall allegedly said, "John Marshall has made his decision; now let him enforce it."

events.title: Triangle Shirtwaist Factory Fire
events.blurb: A fire that broke out in a garment factory occupying the top three floors of a ten-story building in Manhattan's Greenwich Village killed 146 workers — mostly young immigrant women — in less than 18 minutes. Many died because exit doors had been locked from the outside; dozens jumped from the eighth, ninth, and tenth floors to their deaths on the sidewalk below, in full view of horrified onlookers.
events.revealBlurb: March 25, 1911 — Washington Place, New York City. The factory owners were indicted for manslaughter and acquitted, then collected on inflated insurance claims. The disaster triggered passage of more than 30 new labor safety laws in New York State.

events.title: Taft-Hartley Act Becomes Law
events.blurb: The Republican-controlled 80th Congress overrode President Harry Truman's veto, enacting the Labor-Management Relations Act — known as Taft-Hartley — which restricted union activities, banned secondary boycotts and solidarity strikes, permitted states to pass right-to-work laws, and required union officers to swear they were not Communists. The law fundamentally reshaped the relationship between organized labor and the federal government.
events.revealBlurb: June 23, 1947 — Washington, D.C. Truman called it a "slave labor bill" in his veto message, though he later used its provisions himself to break the 1952 steel strike. Union membership peaked at about 35% of the workforce in the late 1940s; by 2024 it had fallen to roughly 10%.

events.title: President Kennedy Assassinated in Dallas
events.blurb: At approximately 12:30 pm that day, President John F. Kennedy was shot in the head while riding in an open motorcade through Dealey Plaza in Dallas, Texas, and was pronounced dead at Parkland Memorial Hospital at 1:00 pm. Lee Harvey Oswald was arrested that afternoon; two days later, Oswald was shot and killed on live national television by nightclub owner Jack Ruby before he could stand trial.
events.revealBlurb: November 22, 1963 — Dallas, Texas. Lyndon Johnson was sworn in as president on Air Force One, with a blood-spattered Jacqueline Kennedy standing beside him. The Warren Commission concluded Oswald acted alone; roughly 60% of Americans have never believed it.

events.title: Battle of Chaeronea
events.blurb: A Macedonian king's army of 32,000 defeated a combined Athenian-Theban force of similar size in central Greece, ending the independence of the classical Greek city-states. The victor's 18-year-old son, commanding the Macedonian left wing, personally broke the famous Sacred Band of Thebes — a unit of 300 elite warrior-lovers who died to the man. The defeat of the city-states unified Greece under Macedonian hegemony and set up the Asian conquests that would follow.
events.revealBlurb: August 338 BCE — King Philip II and his son Alexander. The Sacred Band of Thebes had won every battle it had fought for 40 years; it lost only at Chaeronea. Philip erected a stone lion over their mass grave; the lion, damaged over millennia, was restored in 1902 and still stands there.

events.title: Julius Caesar Assassinated
events.blurb: A Roman dictator, having been named dictator-for-life a month earlier, was stabbed 23 times by a group of 60 senators at a meeting of the Senate held in a Pompey-built theatre. The assassins, styling themselves "Liberators," had convinced themselves that removing the man who had effectively ended the Republic would restore it. Instead, his death plunged Rome into 14 more years of civil war, at the end of which his adopted heir emerged as the first Roman emperor in all but name.
events.revealBlurb: March 15, 44 BCE — the Ides of March. Conspirators included Brutus and Cassius. The supposed last words "Et tu, Brute?" come from Shakespeare; Caesar's actual last words — if he spoke any — may have been the Greek "kai su, teknon?" ("you too, my child?"). His heir Octavian defeated the conspirators at Philippi two years later.

events.title: Battle of Actium
events.blurb: Off the coast of northwestern Greece, Octavian's fleet under Marcus Agrippa met the combined ships of Mark Antony and Cleopatra. When Cleopatra's Egyptian squadron broke off and fled mid-battle, Antony abandoned his own fleet to follow her; his 19 legions on shore surrendered a week later. The last serious rival to a single ruler of Rome was gone.
events.revealBlurb: September 2, 31 BCE. Antony and Cleopatra escaped to Alexandria, where both committed suicide the following year — Antony by falling on his sword (badly), Cleopatra by asp bite (legend) or poison. Octavian kept Cleopatra's son Caesarion alive just long enough to read Caesar's will, then had him killed.

events.title: Hadrian's Wall Begun
events.blurb: A Roman emperor, touring his empire's northern frontier in Britannia, ordered the construction of a 117-kilometre stone-and-turf fortification across the narrow neck of the island from coast to coast. Sixteen forts and dozens of smaller milecastles were strung along it, garrisoned by auxiliary troops from across the empire. It was less a continuous fighting wall than a filter — controlling movement, collecting customs, and projecting imperial authority. Much of it still stands; the wall defined the political frontier for three centuries.
events.revealBlurb: 122 CE — Emperor Hadrian. Construction took six years and employed three legions. Hadrian himself famously declared at the start of his reign that Rome would not continue to expand its borders indefinitely — reversing his predecessor Trajan's conquests in Mesopotamia.

events.title: Sack of Rome by the Visigoths
events.blurb: A Visigothic king and his army, frustrated by failed negotiations with a Western Roman emperor for lands and subsidies, entered Rome itself through an unguarded gate and spent three days pillaging. It was the first time the city had been sacked since the Gauls in 390 BCE — eight centuries earlier. The city's wealth and status had made it symbolically untouchable; the shock rippled through the Mediterranean world. Pagans blamed Rome's adoption of Christianity; Augustine wrote "The City of God" partly in response.
events.revealBlurb: August 24, 410 CE — Alaric I the Visigoth. The emperor Honorius was safely in Ravenna, the western capital since 402. The historian Jerome wrote from Bethlehem: "The city which had taken the whole world was itself taken." Alaric died of illness a few months after the sack.

events.title: Dieppe Raid
events.blurb: Roughly 6,000 troops — mostly Canadians — landed in daylight on a heavily defended beach overlooked by cliffs and were cut down before many could clear the waterline, suffering nearly 60 percent casualties in under ten hours. Planners later claimed the catastrophic failure provided lessons that saved countless lives in subsequent amphibious operations.
events.revealBlurb: August 19, 1942 — Operation Jubilee. Of 4,963 Canadians who embarked, only 2,210 returned to England; 907 were killed and 1,946 taken prisoner. The Germans, who had received advance intelligence, held their positions with minimal effort. Churchill admitted privately it was "a very heavy and grievous loss."

events.title: Birkenau Gas Chambers Operational
events.blurb: Four large purpose-built structures combining undressing rooms, sealed chambers, and industrial crematoria were completed and put into continuous operation at a camp in occupied Poland, creating a killing capacity of several thousand people per day and establishing the industrial infrastructure used to murder the majority of the Holocaust's victims.
events.revealBlurb: The four large crematoria-gas chamber complexes at Auschwitz-Birkenau came fully operational between March and June 1943. At peak operation in the summer of 1944, during the deportation of Hungarian Jews, they killed and cremated up to 10,000 people per day. The Sonderkommando — prisoner workers forced to operate the crematoria — later buried written testimony in the ash.

events.title: Battle of Leyte Gulf
events.blurb: Over four days, 282 warships clashed in four separate engagements across several hundred thousand square kilometres of open ocean — the largest naval battle in history by tonnage and personnel — as one navy committed virtually everything it had left to stop an invasion and the other deployed over 300 ships to press it through.
events.revealBlurb: October 23–26, 1944. Japan used its remaining fleet carriers as decoys with almost no aircraft aboard. A small force of US destroyers and escort carriers somehow bluffed a vastly superior Japanese battleship force into retreating at the Battle of Samar — one of the most improbable tactical reversals of the war. Japan also deployed kamikaze suicide aircraft in force for the first time.

events.title: Battle of the Bulge
events.blurb: 250,000 troops and nearly 1,000 tanks punched through the thinnest part of an Allied front in a snow-covered forested highland, achieving complete surprise and driving a 90-kilometre bulge into the line — the largest land battle ever fought by the United States Army, and the last major offensive Germany would ever launch in the west.
