events.revealBlurb: December 16, 1944 – January 25, 1945. German soldiers wore American uniforms and used captured jeeps to spread chaos behind the lines; dozens were caught and executed. When the surrounded garrison at Bastogne was asked to surrender, Brigadier General Anthony McAuliffe replied with a single word: "Nuts!" The Germans had to ask for a translation.

events.title: Atomic Bombing of Hiroshima
events.blurb: A single aircraft flying at high altitude released a single bomb over a mid-sized city at 8:15 in the morning, detonating it 600 metres above a distinctive T-shaped bridge with the force of 15,000 tons of TNT — flattening 13 square kilometres, killing between 70,000 and 80,000 people instantly, and ultimately causing 140,000 deaths by the end of the year.
events.revealBlurb: August 6, 1945 — B-29 Enola Gay, piloted by Colonel Paul Tibbets, dropped "Little Boy" over Hiroshima. The aiming point was the Aioi Bridge. The bomb missed by about 250 metres but it did not matter. Tibbets's mother's name was Enola Gay. The co-pilot, Robert Lewis, wrote in his journal: "My God, what have we done?"

events.title: Invention of Cuneiform Writing
events.blurb: Administrative workers at a temple complex in one of the world's first cities impressed wedge-shaped marks into wet clay tablets to track grain, livestock, and labor — producing the earliest known writing system. The symbols began as simplified pictures but quickly became abstract signs representing sounds and concepts. Around five thousand of these early tablets have been excavated, most recording the distribution of beer and bread rations to temple workers.
events.revealBlurb: c. 3200 BCE — Uruk, Mesopotamia (modern Iraq). The script evolved over the next millennium into cuneiform, used for Sumerian, Akkadian, Hittite, and a dozen other languages. The oldest known named author in history, the priestess Enheduanna, would write in it a thousand years later.

events.title: Djoser's Step Pyramid Constructed at Saqqara
events.blurb: An architect named Imhotep designed a six-tiered stone structure 62.5 metres tall for his king's burial complex — the first large-scale stone building ever erected. The pyramid was the centerpiece of a 15-hectare mortuary complex enclosed by a paneled limestone wall 10 metres high with 14 false doors and a single real entrance. Imhotep was later deified in his own right, becoming associated with medicine and wisdom.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2650 BCE — Saqqara, Egypt. Pharaoh Djoser, Third Dynasty. Imhotep is one of the first named architects in recorded history. Greeks later identified him with Asclepios, the god of medicine. The pyramid began as a flat mastaba tomb and grew through six successive enlargements.

events.title: Third Dynasty of Ur Founded
events.blurb: A king named Ur-Namma united Mesopotamia after a period of fragmentation and built its most iconic religious structures — stepped pyramid-temples called ziggurats — in every major city. He also issued the oldest surviving law code in history, predating the more famous Babylonian one by three centuries. His successor standardized weights, measures, and the calendar across the entire empire, and administered it through a vast network of clay-tablet bureaucracy.
events.revealBlurb: c. 2112 BCE — Ur, Mesopotamia. Ur-Namma founded the dynasty; his son Shulgi ran it for 48 years with remarkable administrative efficiency. The ziggurat of Ur, built for the moon god Nanna, still stands 30 metres high today — one of the best-preserved structures from the ancient Near East.

events.title: Phoenician Alphabet Comes Into Use
events.blurb: Merchants and scribes along the eastern Mediterranean coast standardized a writing system using 22 consonant letters — the first alphabet with a fixed right-to-left writing direction. The system required no specialist training to learn and could be adapted to write almost any spoken language. It spread rapidly through sea trade to Greece, where vowel letters were added, producing the ancestor of every modern European alphabet.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1050 BCE — Levantine coast (modern Lebanon). The Phoenician alphabet evolved from earlier Proto-Canaanite scripts. The oldest securely dated inscription is on a bronze arrowhead from around 1000 BCE. Within three centuries, adapted versions of this script would be writing Greek, Aramaic, Hebrew, and Arabic.

events.title: Rosetta Stone Decree Issued
events.blurb: A congress of priests convened at Memphis to celebrate a royal coronation and issued a decree granting temple tax exemptions, priestly stipend increases, prisoner amnesty, and renewed support for sacred animal cults. The decree was engraved in two forms of Egyptian script and in Greek onto a granodiorite stele and distributed to temples across the country. The king in whose honor it was issued was thirteen years old.
events.revealBlurb: March 27, 196 BCE — Memphis, Egypt. Ptolemy V Epiphanes. The stele was later carried off by French soldiers in 1799, surrendered to the British, and now sits in the British Museum. Champollion used it in 1822 to crack Egyptian hieroglyphics.

events.title: U.S. Constitution Signed
events.blurb: Fifty-five delegates meeting for four months in a Philadelphia state house, working in secret through a sweltering summer with the windows closed against spies, produced a seven-article document replacing the loose Articles of Confederation with a stronger federal framework. Thirty-nine of them signed. An 81-year-old Benjamin Franklin, who had been at nearly every session, pointed at the sun carved into George Washington's chair and said he was finally sure it was rising, not setting.
events.revealBlurb: September 17, 1787 — Independence Hall, Philadelphia. Ratified June 21, 1788 after New Hampshire became the ninth state to approve. The Constitution has been amended 27 times in 235 years — less than once per decade. A different Philadelphia-era document, the Bill of Rights, followed in 1791.

events.title: Louisiana Purchase Treaty Signed
events.blurb: American negotiators in Paris signed a treaty acquiring roughly 828,000 square miles of territory from France — doubling the size of the United States — for approximately $15 million, or about three cents per acre. The purchase, which Napoleon offered because he needed cash for his European wars, encompassed all or part of fifteen future states and opened the continent to westward expansion.
events.revealBlurb: April 30, 1803 — Paris. Jefferson had only authorized $10 million and was seeking to buy New Orleans alone; Napoleon offered the entire territory. Jefferson privately wondered whether he had constitutional authority to make the deal at all, but bought it anyway. The full price, with interest, came to about $23 million.

events.title: Battle of Austerlitz
events.blurb: A French army of 68,000 men, outnumbered by a combined Russian and Austrian force of 89,000, achieved what is still regarded as one of the greatest tactical victories in military history. Feigning weakness, the French commander baited his opponents into attacking his deliberately weakened right flank, then counter-attacked through the centre as the enemy's lines stretched thin. Three emperors had taken the field; two retreated; the Holy Roman Empire would formally dissolve within a year.
events.revealBlurb: December 2, 1805 — Napoleon's victory over Tsar Alexander I and Emperor Francis II, on the first anniversary of his coronation. The battle is also called "the Battle of the Three Emperors." Allied casualties: ~36,000. French: ~9,000.

events.title: Battle of Leipzig
events.blurb: Four days of fighting around a Saxon city produced the largest battle in European history before World War I, with 600,000 men engaged. A coalition of Russian, Austrian, Prussian, and Swedish forces defeated Napoleon's Grand Army, pressuring a French retreat west over the Rhine. Napoleon had lost Germany; he would lose France within six months. The battle is known in Germany as the Battle of the Nations.
events.revealBlurb: October 16-19, 1813 — Leipzig, Saxony. Casualties: perhaps 100,000 total — roughly 38,000 French, 54,000 Allied. The Battle of Trafalgar eight years earlier had ended French naval power; Leipzig ended French land dominance.

events.title: Revolutions of 1848
events.blurb: Political unrest that had been gathering over economic recession and demands for constitutional government erupted within weeks across most of the European continent, beginning with a winter insurrection in Paris that deposed the king. Vienna, Berlin, Milan, Budapest, Prague, and a dozen other capitals followed within months. Liberals, nationalists, socialists, and workers briefly shared rhetoric; conservatives reorganized and, over the following year, crushed nearly every revolt. The conservative order emerged apparently reinforced — but the political grammar of 19th-century Europe had changed.
events.revealBlurb: February-June 1848 — "The Springtime of Nations." Louis-Philippe of France fled in February; Metternich resigned in Vienna in March. Only France produced lasting regime change, and it soon produced Napoleon III's Second Empire. Karl Marx and Engels published the Communist Manifesto that same February.

events.title: Watt's Separate Condenser Patent
events.blurb: A Scottish instrument maker received a patent for a steam engine design that used a separate condenser chamber, dramatically reducing fuel consumption. Unlike earlier designs that wasted energy reheating the main cylinder on every stroke, the new engine converted roughly 75% more heat into mechanical work.

events.title: Edison Invents Phonograph
events.blurb: A 30-year-old American inventor shouted the first verse of "Mary Had a Little Lamb" into the horn of a machine he had built at his New Jersey laboratory, then cranked a handle to make the machine play his words back to him. Recording sound — not just transmitting it instantaneously as the telephone did — had never been done before. The device, a tinfoil-cylinder phonograph, would be followed by commercial wax-cylinder versions by the end of the decade.
events.revealBlurb: November 21, 1877 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. The original tinfoil phonograph could replay a recording only a few times before the foil wore out. The machine astonished audiences when Edison demonstrated it at the Scientific American office a week later.

events.title: Edison's Practical Lightbulb
events.blurb: After 14 months of systematic experimentation with thousands of possible filament materials — and many previous lightbulb designs by other inventors — an American inventor's laboratory team achieved a 40-hour burn using a carbonized cotton-thread filament in an evacuated glass bulb. The achievement's significance was not inventing the lightbulb itself (which had existed in various forms for decades) but making one that burned long enough to be commercially viable.
events.revealBlurb: October 21, 1879 — Thomas Edison at Menlo Park. His 1880 improved version used a bamboo filament and burned 1,200 hours. Edison's real genius was less invention than the systematic industrial R&D lab he created — the template for every modern corporate research operation.

events.title: Brooklyn Bridge Opens
events.blurb: The longest suspension bridge in the world — 486 metres between its Gothic granite towers — opened to foot and carriage traffic linking Manhattan and Brooklyn across the East River. Its construction had taken 14 years and cost 27 lives. The chief engineer had been paralyzed by decompression sickness while supervising caisson work; his wife Emily had effectively managed the final decade of the project from notes dictated in his sickroom.
events.revealBlurb: May 24, 1883 — designed by John A. Roebling (who died from a dockside accident early in construction). His son Washington Roebling suffered caisson disease and was bedridden; daughter-in-law Emily Warren Roebling led onsite engineering management. She was the first person to cross the completed bridge, in a carriage carrying a rooster.

events.title: Eiffel Tower Opens
events.blurb: A 300-metre wrought-iron lattice tower, built over two years, two months, and five days as the entrance arch to a Paris world's fair, was completed. At three times the height of the Washington Monument, it was the tallest man-made structure in the world and would remain so for 41 years. A petition signed by 300 prominent French artists had protested the "useless and monstrous" project during construction. It was intended to be demolished after 20 years; radio antennas saved it.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1889 — designed by Gustave Eiffel for the 1889 Exposition Universelle, marking the centennial of the French Revolution. It remained the tallest building until the 1930 Chrysler Building. The Nazi occupation cut the elevator cables; Parisians said the "Hitler had to climb the stairs to the top."

events.title: Bach Dedicates Brandenburg Concertos
events.blurb: A 36-year-old German court composer, looking for a new job, sent a margrave a set of six concerto grossi he had been accumulating over several years. The dedication was effusive; he apologized for the "vast distance between his person and the margrave." The margrave never acknowledged the gift, let alone hired him, and probably never had them performed. The manuscripts sat in a Prussian archive for 128 years before rediscovery.
events.revealBlurb: March 24, 1721 — Johann Sebastian Bach, addressing Christian Ludwig of Brandenburg. The scores were narrowly rescued from Allied bombing in 1945. The music now exists thanks to a librarian who grabbed them as he fled Leipzig for the Harz mountains.

events.title: Strange Fruit Recorded
events.blurb: A 23-year-old African-American singer, in a Manhattan studio, recorded a song about the lynching of Black Americans that had been written by a Jewish high-school teacher from the Bronx. Her regular label refused to release it; a tiny specialty label agreed. She closed with it at every set at her Greenwich Village club, the room going dark except for a spotlight on her face, no encore permitted. The song haunted her for the rest of her short life.
events.revealBlurb: April 20, 1939 — Billie Holiday, Commodore Records. Songwriter: Abel Meeropol, under the pen name Lewis Allan. Meeropol and his wife later adopted the two young sons of the executed Ethel and Julius Rosenberg.

events.title: Beatles' Final Public Performance
events.blurb: A four-piece rock band performed without announcement on the roof of their recording company's London headquarters for 42 minutes in near-freezing winter temperatures, drawing a crowd of hundreds in the street below before police ended the show citing noise complaints. The impromptu rooftop set was their last performance together in front of a live audience.

events.title: Bob Marley's Exodus Released
events.blurb: A Jamaican reggae star, recovering in a London flat after being shot in an assassination attempt at his home five months earlier, released his ninth studio album. Its tracks — "Three Little Birds," "One Love," "Jamming," "Waiting in Vain," and the title track — would become the core of his international legacy. Time magazine named it the album of the century. He had fled to London for his safety; the exile shaped the record.
events.revealBlurb: June 3, 1977 — Bob Marley and the Wailers. The album was recorded at Island Studios in London. The attempted assassination on December 3, 1976 had injured him, his wife, and his manager. Marley would die of cancer at 36 in 1981.

events.title: Live Aid
events.blurb: Two simultaneous 16-hour benefit concerts, one at a stadium in London and one at a stadium in Philadelphia, were broadcast live to an estimated 1.9 billion people in 150 countries — at the time perhaps 40 percent of the world population. The concerts raised around $127 million for Ethiopian famine relief. A British band's 21-minute set, by most accounts, stole the whole day. Its lead singer's synchronized clap-along with 72,000 people is the stuff of legend.
events.revealBlurb: July 13, 1985 — Wembley Stadium and JFK Stadium. The stealing-the-show band was Queen, Freddie Mercury at Wembley. Co-organizers Bob Geldof and Midge Ure. "Feed the World" had been launched by the Band Aid charity single the previous Christmas.

events.title: FIFA Founded
events.blurb: Representatives of seven European national football associations — Belgium, Denmark, France, Netherlands, Spain, Sweden, and Switzerland — met at a Paris sports association's offices and established an international governing body for the sport. England, which had invented the modern codified game and considered itself the natural authority, declined to attend, joined in 1905, and withdrew multiple times over subsequent decades in petty disputes. The organization would run the World Cup from 1930 on.
events.revealBlurb: May 21, 1904 — Fédération Internationale de Football Association, Paris. Its first president was Robert Guérin. FIFA now has 211 member associations, more than the UN. Its headquarters moved to Zurich in 1932 and have been there since.

events.title: Mark Spitz Wins Seventh Munich Gold
events.blurb: An American swimmer won his seventh gold medal of the Munich Games by anchoring the 4×100-metre medley relay team, setting a world record in every individual event he entered. No athlete had ever won more gold medals at a single Olympic Games, and he set or broke a world record in each of his seven finals.

events.title: Secretariat Wins the Triple Crown
events.blurb: A three-year-old chestnut colt won the Belmont Stakes by 31 lengths in a world-record time of 2 minutes 24 seconds, becoming the first Triple Crown winner in 25 years. His margin of victory and track record remain unmatched; television viewers watching the broadcast described the race as looking like a different event from the others.

events.title: India Wins Cricket World Cup
events.blurb: The Indian men's cricket team won their second-ever Cricket World Cup, beating Sri Lanka by six wickets in the final at a Mumbai stadium in front of a home crowd that included the country's most beloved cricketer, who was playing in his sixth and final World Cup. The tournament winner's 36-year-old captain carried the little master on his shoulders around the stadium in celebration. It was the first time any nation had won a World Cup final on its own soil.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 2011 — India beat Sri Lanka at Wankhede Stadium, Mumbai. Captain MS Dhoni hit the winning six. Sachin Tendulkar's 28 runs in his final-ever ODI innings on the way to the trophy saw him carried on teammates' shoulders around the stadium.

events.title: Kobe Bryant Dies
events.blurb: A 41-year-old retired basketball star, his 13-year-old daughter, and seven other passengers died when their private helicopter crashed into a hillside in thick fog outside Los Angeles while en route to a youth basketball game. The retired player had won five NBA championships, two Olympic golds, and the nickname "Black Mamba" during a 20-year career entirely with the Los Angeles Lakers. The crash prompted an outpouring of mourning around the world.
events.revealBlurb: January 26, 2020 — Kobe and Gianna Bryant. National Transportation Safety Board findings attributed the crash to pilot error in poor visibility. His 2017 jersey-retirement ceremony at Staples Center saw both his numbers (8 and 24) raised to the rafters — the only player in franchise history with multiple retired numbers.

events.title: Parthenon Marbles Completed
events.blurb: Under the direction of a single master sculptor, a team of Athenian craftsmen completed the exterior sculptural programme of a temple on a fortified limestone hill above their city — a continuous carved frieze 160 metres long depicting a civic religious procession, plus 92 metopes and two pediments. The sculptures were painted in vivid colours; the bleached white appearance known to modern viewers is an accident of weathering.
events.revealBlurb: c. 438 BCE — Phidias, chief sculptor of the Parthenon in Athens. Lord Elgin removed about half the surviving marbles between 1801 and 1812 and sold them to the British Museum. Greece has been asking for them back for over 200 years.

events.title: Terracotta Army Created
events.blurb: In a pit 1.5 kilometres east of the tomb of a Chinese emperor who had just died, labourers arranged some 8,000 life-sized clay soldiers, 130 chariots, and 670 horses facing east, ready to defend him in the afterlife. Each soldier's face was modelled individually; no two are identical. The figures had originally been painted in bright colours that flaked off within days of excavation when exposed to dry modern air.
events.revealBlurb: c. 210 BCE — the tomb of Qin Shi Huang, first emperor of unified China. Rediscovered by local farmers drilling a well in March 1974. The emperor's own tomb mound remains unexcavated — ancient sources describe rivers of mercury; soil tests confirm unusual mercury levels.

events.title: Giotto's Arena Chapel Frescoes
events.blurb: A Florentine painter completed a fresco cycle covering the interior walls of a small private chapel in a northern Italian city, commissioned by a banker trying to atone for his father's usury. The artist's naturalistic figures, three-dimensional space, and emotional humanism broke decisively with Byzantine conventions and set the visual vocabulary of the next three centuries. Vasari would later date the start of the Renaissance from his work.
events.revealBlurb: 1305 — Giotto di Bondone, at the Scrovegni (Arena) Chapel in Padua. Enrico Scrovegni built the chapel on the site of a Roman arena, and commissioned the frescoes to atone for the soul of his father, named in Dante's Inferno.

events.title: Hokusai's Great Wave
events.blurb: A 70-year-old Japanese printmaker produced the first of thirty-six woodblock prints depicting views of a sacred mountain, all showing it from different perspectives and in different weather. The first print, which viewers sometimes mistook for the title piece, showed an enormous wave curling in threatening foam over three small fishing boats, with the mountain a distant cone between its spray. The distinctive blue pigment, Prussian blue, was a recent European import.
events.revealBlurb: c. 1831 — Katsushika Hokusai. The print is one of the most widely reproduced images in the world; thousands of impressions survive. Hokusai called himself "the old man mad about drawing" and claimed he would become a true artist only at 110.

events.title: Duchamp's Fountain
events.blurb: A French artist submitted an ordinary porcelain urinal, signed with a pseudonym and dated, as a sculpture entitled "Fountain" to the first exhibition of New York's Society of Independent Artists. The Society's board — of which he was a member — voted after heated debate to reject it. He resigned in protest. The original object was lost; the artist authorized 17 replicas over subsequent decades, each now valued at millions.
events.revealBlurb: April 1917 — Marcel Duchamp, signed "R. Mutt 1917." The original was photographed by Alfred Stieglitz and then disappeared. A 2004 survey of 500 art-world professionals named it the most influential artwork of the 20th century. An artist attacked a replica with a hammer in 2006.

events.title: Nintendo NES Released in US
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company launched, in a limited New York test market, a home video-game console — two years after it had flopped in its first US release attempt under the brand name Advanced Video System. The relaunched system came with a new console design, a "Zapper" light gun, a robotic companion, and a launch bundle including Super Mario Bros. The North American video game market had collapsed in 1983; the Nintendo relaunch is widely credited with reviving it.
events.revealBlurb: October 18, 1985 — Nintendo Entertainment System (NES). The Japanese original ("Famicom") had launched in July 1983. R.O.B. the robot's inclusion was marketing cleverness to avoid "video game" retailer resistance — the NES was pitched initially as a toy. By 1988, 7 million units had sold.

events.title: Seinfeld Premieres
events.blurb: A 90-minute pilot episode titled "The Seinfeld Chronicles" aired on NBC, starring a 35-year-old New York stand-up comedian as a fictionalized version of himself and three friends navigating petty social minutiae in Manhattan. NBC had almost dropped the show; test audiences had responded coolly. A show famously about "nothing," it would run 180 episodes over nine seasons and become one of the most influential sitcoms in television history.
events.revealBlurb: July 5, 1989 — Jerry Seinfeld, Jason Alexander, Michael Richards (Julia Louis-Dreyfus joined season 2). Co-creator Larry David later made Curb Your Enthusiasm, essentially a Seinfeld-universe spinoff. The cast famously turned down $5 million per episode each to continue past season 9.

events.title: Kurt Cobain Dies
events.blurb: A 27-year-old grunge-rock frontman was found dead of a self-inflicted shotgun wound in the greenhouse above the garage of his Seattle home. He had struggled with heroin addiction, a collapsed marriage, chronic stomach pain, and the deep anxieties of sudden fame. His suicide note quoted a line from a Neil Young song: "It's better to burn out than to fade away." A public memorial at Seattle Center drew 7,000 mourners.
events.revealBlurb: April 5, 1994 — Kurt Cobain of Nirvana. The body was not discovered for three days, by an electrician installing a security system. Conspiracy theories have persisted for decades. Cobain joined the "27 Club" of pop musicians who died at that age, including Jimi Hendrix, Janis Joplin, Jim Morrison, and Amy Winehouse.

events.title: Tamagotchi Released
events.blurb: A Japanese toy company released a small egg-shaped plastic keychain with a tiny LCD screen and three buttons. The device simulated a virtual pet that needed feeding, playing with, and cleaning up after — with beeps demanding attention at all hours, including in the middle of lessons in schools. Schools banned them. 40 million units sold globally. The craze prefigured the attention-hijacking mobile apps of decades later.
events.revealBlurb: November 23, 1996 — Bandai. Designed by Akihiro Yokoi and Aki Maita. Later versions could be put to sleep or paused; the original would simply "die" if neglected, and the keychain had to be reset. The name combines Japanese "tamago" (egg) and "watch."

events.title: Titanic Premieres in the US
events.blurb: A three-hour romantic drama set aboard a doomed ocean liner's maiden voyage opened in American cinemas after a $200 million production budget — then the most expensive film ever made. It held the record as the highest-grossing film in history for twelve years and was the first to earn $1 billion and later $2 billion worldwide.

events.title: NATO Founded
events.blurb: Twelve nations from both sides of the Atlantic signed a mutual defense treaty in Washington, D.C., committing that an armed attack against one would be considered an attack against all. The alliance was built around Article 5 — a collective defense clause that has been invoked exactly once in its history, after 9/11.
events.revealBlurb: April 4, 1949 — founding members included the US, UK, France, Canada, and eight others. Lord Ismay, its first Secretary General, quipped its purpose was "to keep the Russians out, the Americans in, and the Germans down."

events.title: McCarthy Wheeling Speech
events.blurb: At a Lincoln Day dinner in West Virginia, a previously obscure U.S. senator brandished a piece of paper and claimed it listed 205 known communists working in the State Department. The charge, later revised repeatedly and never substantiated, launched a four-year domestic witch-hunt that would bear his name.
events.revealBlurb: February 9, 1950 — Joseph McCarthy, up for re-election, stumbled onto his signature issue. The "list" he waved kept changing: 205, then 57, then 81. No copy of the original was ever produced. It destroyed thousands of careers anyway.

events.title: Helsinki Accords
events.blurb: Thirty-five nations — every European country except tiny Albania, plus the U.S. and Canada — signed a sweeping final act in the Finnish capital that acknowledged post-war borders while binding signatories to respect human rights. Critics called it a sellout to Moscow. In fact, its human rights provisions gave eastern dissidents a legal framework that would undermine the regimes a decade later.
events.revealBlurb: August 1, 1975 — the "Third Basket" on human rights proved subversive. Czech dissidents founded Charter 77 using its language; the Moscow Helsinki Group followed. Brezhnev didn't realize he'd just signed his system's eventual death warrant.

events.title: SDI Announced
events.blurb: In a televised address from the Oval Office, a U.S. president proposed a space-based missile defense shield intended to render nuclear weapons "impotent and obsolete." Critics dubbed it "Star Wars" and scientists called it technically unachievable. Whatever its technical merits, the announcement terrified the Kremlin and forced Soviet planners to contemplate a ruinous new arms race they could not afford.
events.revealBlurb: March 23, 1983 — Reagan's Strategic Defense Initiative. It never produced a working system, but it contributed to Soviet economic exhaustion. Some historians credit SDI with accelerating Gorbachev's arms-control pivot by years.

events.title: Soviet Union Dissolves
events.blurb: In a televised resignation speech, the last leader of a superpower announced the end of his office and, by implication, the end of the 69-year-old multinational state he had led for six and a half years. The hammer-and-sickle flag was lowered above the Kremlin for the final time and replaced with the Russian tricolor. Fifteen newly independent countries inherited the ruins.
events.revealBlurb: December 25, 1991 — Mikhail Gorbachev's resignation. The USSR formally ceased to exist the next day. Gorbachev lived another 31 years, mostly ignored at home and celebrated abroad, occasionally appearing in Pizza Hut and Louis Vuitton ads.

events.title: Metropolis Released
events.blurb: A 36-year-old Austrian director released a 153-minute silent epic — at the time the most expensive film ever made — set in a stratified future city where wealthy elites enjoy skyscraper gardens above an underground inferno of machine-tending workers. The film's visual language — robot maidens, neon skylines, expressionist sets — shaped science-fiction imagery for the next century. The premiere had uneven reception; 40 minutes of footage were later cut.
events.revealBlurb: January 10, 1927 — Fritz Lang at the UFA-Palast am Zoo, Berlin. A reasonably complete version was pieced together only in 2008, when a 16mm print from the 1930s was found in a Buenos Aires archive. The robot Maria was voted the most important film robot in history.

events.title: First Academy Awards
events.blurb: A 15-minute banquet at a Hollywood hotel awarded twelve statuettes — a 34 cm tall gilded figure of a knight standing on a reel of film — to films, actors, directors, and technicians selected by the newly formed Academy of Motion Picture Arts and Sciences. 270 people attended. The winners had been announced three months earlier. The whole ceremony received brief mention in the next day's Los Angeles Times, on page 10.
events.revealBlurb: May 16, 1929 — Hollywood Roosevelt Hotel. First Best Picture: "Wings." Best Actor: Emil Jannings. The bronze statuette's nickname, "Oscar," was supposedly coined by an Academy librarian who thought it resembled her Uncle Oscar; the story is almost certainly retrofitted.

events.title: 2001: A Space Odyssey Released
events.blurb: A 39-year-old New York-born director released a 149-minute science-fiction film about human evolution, artificial intelligence, and alien contact, with minimal dialogue, a four-movement structure, and long classical-music sequences of spacecraft slowly docking to the Blue Danube. The first audience walked out in droves; reviews were mixed. Within two years, it was the highest-grossing film of its year and had reshaped what cinema was permitted to do.
events.revealBlurb: April 2, 1968 — Stanley Kubrick. Co-written with Arthur C. Clarke. The jump cut from a primeval bone thrown into the air to a spaceship in orbit covers 4 million years in one frame. HAL 9000's voice was performed by Canadian Shakespearean actor Douglas Rain.

events.title: The Matrix Released
events.blurb: Two siblings who had directed only one feature between them released a 136-minute science-fiction film in which the world turns out to be a computer simulation and humanity is harvested by machines as a power source. The film's "bullet time" effect — a camera arcing around a frozen-mid-action character while the world resumed behind it — became an instantly iconic technique. Its cyberpunk philosophy, couture, and green-tinted aesthetic defined the turn of the millennium.
events.revealBlurb: March 31, 1999 — Lana and Lilly Wachowski, starring Keanu Reeves. "Bullet time" was achieved with a ring of 120 still cameras. The concept of a simulated reality — the "red pill / blue pill" — has since migrated into every internet conspiracy subculture.

events.title: Moonlight/La La Land Envelope Mix-Up
events.blurb: At a televised U.S. film industry awards ceremony, presenters opened the wrong envelope and declared a popular musical romance the Best Picture winner. Its producers took the stage, began delivering speeches, and accepted their statuettes before an increasingly visible commotion behind them revealed the mistake. The actual winner was announced with two minutes of live-broadcast awkwardness remaining. It was the first Best Picture with an all-Black cast.
events.revealBlurb: February 26, 2017 — Moonlight, directed by Barry Jenkins. Warren Beatty and Faye Dunaway had been handed the wrong envelope. Jenkins later said: "I saw the envelope. I know what I saw." The accounting firm PwC, responsible for the envelopes, took the blame.
